## Self-Similarity Matrices

A Self-Similarity Matrix (SSM) compares every moment in a track with every other moment, producing a visual map of structural repetition and contrast. By computing SSMs from both chroma (harmonic) and timbre (textural) features, we can examine whether a track's form is driven by harmonic development or by changes in sound texture.

## Harmonic Structure: Wood

<div style="text-align:center;">
  <img src="Rplot01.png" style="max-width:600px;width:100%;height:auto;">
</div>

The chroma-based self-similarity matrix of *Wood* displays a clear block-diagonal structure, with well-defined rectangular regions along the main diagonal. Each block represents a section of the track where harmonic content remains internally consistent, and the sharp transitions between blocks indicate structural boundaries. This confirms that *Wood* is composed of **discrete, recurring harmonic zones** rather than continuous development — typical of loop-based electronic music where form emerges through the layering and removal of elements over a repeating harmonic foundation.

## Chroma vs Timbre: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Chroma
<div style="text-align:center;"><img src="Rplot02.png" style="max-width:600px;width:100%;height:auto;"></div>

### Timbre
<div style="text-align:center;"><img src="Rplot03.png" style="max-width:600px;width:100%;height:auto;"></div>

:::

Comparing the two SSMs reveals that harmonic and timbral structure can diverge significantly within the same track. The **chroma SSM** shows clean, well-defined repetition blocks: the chorus chord progressions return predictably, producing a regular checkerboard-like pattern. The **timbre SSM**, by contrast, is noisier and more irregular — even during harmonically identical sections, the texture shifts as vocal intensity varies, drum patterns change, and the arrangement evolves. This demonstrates that a track can be **harmonically stable** while remaining **texturally dynamic**, and that chroma and timbre illuminate fundamentally different dimensions of musical structure. Using only one of these features would give an incomplete picture.
